lesson.title: Why Every Invertible Function Has a Differentiable Inverse (Usually)
lesson.summary: The Inverse Function Theorem says that if f is differentiable and invertible near a point with f'(x) not zero there, then f inverse is differentiable too, and its derivative is the reciprocal of f's.
lesson.body:
Suppose f is a differentiable, one-to-one function (prerequisite: inverse function) near some point a, so its inverse f^{-1} exists near b = f(a). Does f^{-1} have a derivative there, and if so, what is it? The cleanest way to answer this is with a technique you already have: implicit differentiation.

Let y = f^{-1}(x). By the definition of an inverse function, this is exactly the same statement as f(y) = x. That is an implicit equation relating y and x, no different in kind from the circles and curves in the earlier chapters of this unit. Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The left side needs the chain rule, treating y as a function of x: d/dx[f(y)] = f'(y) (dy/dx). The right side is d/dx[x] = 1. So:

f'(y) (dy/dx) = 1, which gives dy/dx = 1/f'(y) = 1/f'(f^{-1}(x))

This is the Inverse Function Theorem: (f^{-1})'(x) = 1/f'(f^{-1}(x)), valid wherever f'(f^{-1}(x)) is not zero. Check it on a function simple enough to verify both ways: f(x) = x^3, with f'(x) = 3x^2. At x = 2, f(2) = 8 and f'(2) = 3(4) = 12, so the theorem predicts (f^{-1})'(8) = 1/12. Since f^{-1}(x) = x^{1/3} here, its derivative is (1/3) x^{-2/3}; at x = 8, that is (1/3)(1/4) = 1/12, because 8^{2/3} = (8^{1/3})^2 = 2^2 = 4. The two answers match.

The hypothesis f'(x) not zero is not a technicality. At x0 = 0, f'(0) = 3(0)^2 = 0, and indeed f^{-1}(x) = x^{1/3} has a vertical tangent line at x = 0, its derivative (1/3) x^{-2/3} blows up as x approaches 0. When f's tangent line is flat, the reflected tangent line for f^{-1} is vertical, and a vertical line has no slope to report.
